newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil rates seen stable despite room to cut.
newsitem.headline: Brazil rates seen stable despite room to cut.

text.p: Brazil will probably leave interest rates unchanged this week despite low inflation rates and weaker economic growth which has opened some room to cut, economists said.

"There is technical space for a reduction in rates. But this is not a good moment because it would be the first decision by (new Central Bank chief Gustavo) Franco and if he comes in changing rates, even if he lowers them, then it might make the markets nervous," said Roberto Padovani, an economist at the consulting firm Trend Analise.
The Central Bank's Monetary Policy Committee meets Wednesday to set September interest rates. Franco will be sworn in as new Central Bank president before the meeting.

The committee has not changed monthly interest rates since April, when it set its basic interest rate, the TBC, at 1.58 percent and its basic assistance rate, the TBAN, at 1.78 percent. The two rates roughly act as a floor and ceiling for market interest rates.
"We think they will keep rates the same, and that a cut will only come in the last quarter of the year," Banco Santander said in a statement.

In addition to Franco's inauguration, economists noted that the market would still be looking at continued turmoil in Asian currency markets. Although recent capital flows to Brazil have been strong, economists said policymakers may not want to risk any lowering of rates amid the current volatility in Asian emerging markets.

Still, economists acknowledged that a number of factors made a slight easing possible. First, inflation forecasts for the year have fallen sharply thanks to a warm winter, which has slashed clothing and food prices on high inventories and strong agricultural output.
Inflation forecasts for 1997 have fallen over the past two weeks to about 5.5 percent from 7.0-8.0 percent at the beginning of the year.

In addition, most economists are lowering economic growth forecasts for the year to the 3.0-3.5 percent range from 4.0-4.5 percent, confident that the once-feared "overheating" will not materialize this year.
Finally, the U.S. Federal Reserve Board was widely seen leaving short-term interest rates unchanged on Tuesday, which would free up Brazilian policymakers to cut local rates.
These factors have led many in the market to give a cut of two basis points a fifty-fifty chance versus leaving rates unchanged.

"If I had to bet I would say they will cut the TBC to 1.56 percent for September. And if they don't do it now, then they will almost certainly do it next month for the October rate," said Odair Abate, chief economist for Lloyds Bank in Brazil.
A Reuter survey of eight Brazilian banks and research firms forecast monthly interest rates to end the year at 1.62 percent.
